course.name: Islamic Humanities
course.tagline: Map game, timeline, key figures and their works.

cards.simple: The community of Muslim believers as a whole, across tribe, ethnicity and place.
Muhammad’s emigration from Mecca to Medina (Yathrib) in 622. It marks year 1 of the Islamic (AH) calendar and the start of the first Muslim polity.
The scripture of Islam, believed by Muslims to be God’s word revealed to Muhammad (c. 610–632). 114 suras (chapters), in Arabic.
more: Its literary Arabic became the reference standard for the language and for later literature.

cards.simple: Hadith: reports of what Muhammad said, did or approved, each with a chain of transmitters (isnad). Sunna: his normative practice, known largely through hadith.
Shahada (profession of faith), salat (prayer five times a day), zakat (obligatory alms), sawm (fasting in Ramadan), hajj (pilgrimage to Mecca, once if able).
Khalifa, “successor” (or deputy): the leader of the Muslim community after Muhammad. Rashidun (632–661), then Umayyad and Abbasid dynasties.

It began as a dispute over who should lead after Muhammad. Shi‘is (“partisans” of ‘Ali) hold that leadership belonged to ‘Ali and his descendants, the Imams. Karbala (680) became its defining tragedy.
Sharia: the divine law/path in principle. Fiqh: human jurisprudence, the scholars’ effort to derive rulings from the Qur’an, sunna, consensus (ijma‘) and analogy (qiyas).
The learned scholars of religion and law: jurists, judges (qadis), teachers and muftis. They often mediated between rulers and the people.
A college of religious and legal learning. Spread widely from the 11th century, notably the Seljuk vizier Nizam al-Mulk’s Nizamiyya madrasas.
A charitable endowment: property whose income is dedicated in perpetuity to a purpose such as a mosque, madrasa, hospital or fountain.
more: The financial backbone of much of the premodern Islamic world’s education and welfare.

cards.simple: Dhimmis: protected non-Muslim communities (Jews, Christians and others) under Muslim rule, with communal autonomy. They paid a poll tax, the jizya.
In Abbasid Baghdad (8th–10th c.), Greek, Persian and Indian works in philosophy, medicine, mathematics and astronomy were translated into Arabic, often through Syriac.
Falsafa: philosophy in the Greek (Aristotelian/Neoplatonic) tradition: al-Kindi, al-Farabi, Ibn Sina, Ibn Rushd. Kalam: rational, dialectical theology defending doctrine (Mu‘tazilis, Ash‘aris).
The mystical dimension of Islam: seeking direct experience of God through devotion, remembrance (dhikr) and discipline, often organized in orders (tariqas) around a master.
Capital Damascus. Expanded from Iberia to Central Asia; Arabic became the language of administration; built the Dome of the Rock. A branch ruled al-Andalus from Córdoba (756–1031).
Came to power in a revolution based in Khurasan; founded Baghdad (762). Golden age of learning; real power later fragmented. Ended in Baghdad with the Mongol sack of 1258.
Slave-soldiers who became rulers. The Mamluk sultanate (Egypt and Syria, 1250–1517) stopped the Mongols at ‘Ayn Jalut (1260) and was conquered by the Ottomans in 1517.
Ottoman (c. 1299–1922, Istanbul from 1453), Safavid (1501–1736, made Twelver Shi‘ism the state religion; Isfahan), Mughal (1526–1857, Delhi/Agra).
The Ottoman levy of Christian boys, converted and trained for the Janissary infantry or palace and state service.
Ottoman arrangement in which religious communities (e.g. Greek Orthodox, Armenian, Jewish) ran their own personal-status law and internal affairs under their leaders.
The classical Arabic ode: a long monorhyme poem, traditionally opening with a nostalgic prelude (nasib) at an abandoned campsite before a journey and a main theme such as praise.
A shorter lyric love poem in monorhyme. Central to Persian poetry (Hafez), where earthly and divine love often blur.
Refined culture and etiquette, and the literature of the cultivated person: anthologies, belles-lettres, wit and moral instruction.
Honeycomb or “stalactite” vaulting built from tiers of small niches. Used in domes, portals and transitions (e.g. the Alhambra).
Infinitely extendable patterns of scrolling, interlacing vegetal forms, alongside geometric patterns and calligraphy in Islamic ornament.

Mihrab: niche marking the qibla (direction of Mecca). Minbar: stepped pulpit for the Friday sermon. Minaret: tower for the call to prayer. Iwan: vaulted hall open on one side (key in Iranian mosques).
Ottoman reform era: centralization, legal equality of subjects regardless of religion, new courts, schools and codes on European models.
The Arab “awakening/renaissance” of the 19th and early 20th centuries: printing, journalism, translation, new literary forms and the revival of classical Arabic.
Late 19th-century reform movement (al-Afghani, Muhammad ‘Abduh) arguing that Islam is compatible with reason, science and modern institutions.
Secret Anglo-French agreement dividing the Ottoman Arab lands into spheres of influence. It shaped the post-WWI mandates and is a lasting symbol of colonial borders.
Edward Said’s argument that Western scholarship, art and literature constructed “the Orient” as an exotic, inferior Other, a body of knowledge entangled with imperial power.

questions.label: Q1
questions.prompt: An 11th-century Baghdad merchant permanently dedicates the rent from his shops to pay teachers at a new school. What legal instrument is he using?

options.why: A perpetual charitable endowment, which typically funded madrasas, mosques and hospitals.
Zakat is the obligatory annual alms, not a permanent endowment of property.
The poll tax paid by dhimmis.
A fatwa is a legal opinion by a mufti, not a property arrangement.

questions.label: Q2
questions.prompt: A jurist works out whether a new kind of contract is permitted by reasoning from the Qur’an, hadith, scholarly consensus and analogy. This activity is…

options.why: Jurisprudence: the human effort to derive rulings. Consensus (ijma‘) and analogy (qiyas) are among its sources.
Kalam is dialectical theology (God’s attributes, free will), not legal rulings.
Philosophy in the Greek tradition.
Tafsir is Qur’an commentary. It can feed into law but isn’t the derivation of rulings itself.

questions.label: Q3
questions.prompt: An octagonal shrine with a gilded dome over a rock outcrop in Jerusalem, built under the Umayyad caliph ‘Abd al-Malik around 691–692.

options.why: The earliest major surviving Islamic monument.
Al-Aqsa is the nearby congregational mosque on the same platform, rectangular in plan.
Also Umayyad (early 8th c.), but in Damascus, built under al-Walid I.
A 6th-century Byzantine church in Constantinople, converted to a mosque in 1453.

questions.label: Q4
questions.prompt: Tiers of small, stacked niches forming a honeycomb-like vault, famous in the Alhambra’s halls.

options.why: The “stalactite” vaulting typical of Islamic architecture from the 11th–12th c. on.
Arabesque is flat, scrolling vegetal ornament, not three-dimensional vaulting.
An iwan is a single large vaulted hall open on one side.
The niche showing the direction of prayer. It can contain muqarnas but is a different thing.

questions.label: Q5
questions.prompt: A Safavid mosque in Isfahan’s great square with no minaret and no courtyard, built for the royal household (early 17th c.).

options.why: Its unusual plan reflects its use as a private royal mosque.
Also on the square, but a congregational mosque with minarets, iwans and a courtyard.
Ottoman, in Istanbul, with six minarets.
A Mughal mausoleum in Agra, not a mosque in Isfahan.

questions.label: Q6
questions.prompt: An early 17th-century Ottoman mosque in Istanbul, unusual for having six minarets.

options.why: Built 1609–1616 for Sultan Ahmed I. Its blue İznik tiles gave the nickname.
Sinan’s masterpiece of the 1550s, with four minarets.
Sinan’s late masterpiece, but in Edirne (1570s).
Its minarets were added after 1453 and there are four.

questions.label: Q7
questions.prompt: Ibn Khaldun explains the rise and fall of dynasties through a group’s cohesion, which is strong among desert peoples and weakened by luxury. He calls it…

options.why: Group solidarity, the engine of his cyclical theory in the Muqaddima.
The whole community of believers, not tribal solidarity.
Consensus of scholars, a source of law.
Blessing or spiritual power, often linked to saints.

options.t: The Mongols sacked Baghdad, ending the Abbasid caliphate there
options.why: Hülegü’s army killed the caliph al-Musta‘sim.
That was 1453.
That was 680.

options.t: Granada fell to Castile and Aragon
options.why: That was 1492.

questions.label: Q9
questions.prompt: The Sunni–Shi‘i divide began as a disagreement about…

options.t: Who should lead the community after Muhammad
options.why: Shi‘is backed ‘Ali and his descendants. Theological and legal differences grew later.
Both share the same Qur’an.
Both pray toward Mecca.
Sufism exists in both traditions and isn’t the origin of the split.

questions.label: Q10
questions.prompt: The Ottoman practice of levying Christian boys to be converted and trained for the Janissaries and state service is called…

options.why: The “collection”.
The system of self-governing religious communities.
A land-revenue grant supporting a cavalryman.
The 19th-century reforms.

questions.label: Q11
questions.prompt: A short monorhyme love lyric, in which earthly and divine love often blur, perfected in Persian by Hafez.

options.why: Hafez’s Divan is the classic collection of ghazals.
The longer, multi-part ode, often panegyric.
A quatrain (four lines), the form of Omar Khayyam’s Rubaiyat.
Long narrative poetry in rhyming couplets, like Rumi’s Masnavi.

options.t: Western representations of “the Orient” constructed it as an inferior Other, entangled with imperial power
options.why: Knowledge and power reinforce each other.

options.t: Middle Eastern societies were unchanged for centuries
options.why: That’s the kind of claim Said criticizes.

options.t: Orientalist painters were the most accurate observers of the Middle East
options.why: He treats their images as projections, not documents.

options.t: The Ottoman Empire collapsed because of Sufism
options.why: Not his subject.

questions.label: Q13
questions.prompt: Year 1 of the Islamic (AH) calendar corresponds to…

options.why: The calendar counts from the emigration, the founding of the community.
The calendar starts from the hijra, not his birth.
An important date, but not the calendar’s start.
That year begins the caliphate, not the calendar.

questions.label: Q14
questions.prompt: The 19th-century Arab literary and cultural revival of printing, journalism and new literary forms is called…

options.why: “Awakening” or “renaissance”.
The Ottoman state reforms (1839–1876).
The pre-Islamic “age of ignorance”.
The Christian conquest of al-Andalus.
